about: Programming 1 (ELEC0007) is a 7.5-credit Term 2 module in UCL's Department of Electronic and Electrical Engineering that teaches basic and intermediate programming in C, aimed at the programming electrical engineers need for microcontrollers, robotics and AI-based electronic systems. Its 2026/27 catalogue entry lists outcomes running from compiling a first program, types, arrays, structs, loops, conditionals and functions to pointers, malloc and free, linked lists and binary trees, and running code on a microcontroller; this pack follows that order. The module is taught in person and, per the 2026/27 catalogue, assessed 100% by exam. The catalogue does not say which microcontroller board is used, so the embedded topic here is kept general.
topics: Compiling and running a C program
Pointers; pass by value vs reference

notes.h: From source file to running program
notes.body:
C is a compiled language: you write human-readable source code in a .c file, and a toolchain turns it into machine code that the processor runs directly. Knowing what each stage does helps you read error messages quickly, which is a skill exam questions often test.

A minimal program
    #include <stdio.h>

    int main(void)
    {
        printf("Hello, EEE!\n");
        return 0;
    }

- #include <stdio.h> pastes in the declarations of the standard input/output functions, including printf.
- Every program starts executing at main. It returns an int to the operating system: 0 means success, a non-zero value signals an error.
- Statements end with a semicolon; braces group statements into blocks.
- Comments are written /* like this */ or // like this.

Building it
On a Linux or macOS terminal with gcc:
    gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra hello.c -o hello
    ./hello
-Wall and -Wextra switch on useful warnings; treat warnings as bugs until you are sure they are harmless. -o names the output file.

The four stages
- Preprocessing: handles lines starting with #. #include copies a header file in, #define replaces macro names with text. gcc -E stops here.
- Compilation: checks syntax and types and translates C into assembly language for the target processor. gcc -S stops here and writes a .s file.
- Assembly: turns assembly into machine code in an object file (.o). gcc -c stops here, so it compiles without linking.
- Linking: combines your object files with library code (for example the real printf) and produces the executable.

Three kinds of error
- Compile-time errors: a missing semicolon, an undeclared variable, the wrong number of arguments. No executable is produced.
- Link-time errors: everything compiled, but the linker cannot find a function's definition, typically shown as "undefined reference to ...". A misspelt function name causes this, and so does forgetting a library: with gcc on many Linux systems the maths functions in math.h (sqrt, sin, pow) need -lm at the end of the command.
- Run-time errors: the program runs but crashes (for example a segmentation fault from a bad pointer) or gives wrong answers (a logic error).

Input and output
- printf uses format specifiers: %d for int, %f for double, %c for char, %s for a string, %x for hexadecimal, %p for a pointer, %zu for a size_t value such as the result of sizeof.
- scanf("%d", &x) reads an int into x; it needs the address of x (the & operator), because it has to change x. scanf returns the number of items it successfully read, so check it.

Exam tips: be able to name the stage at which a given error appears, and remember that a header declares a function while a library supplies its compiled code.

Every variable in C has a type, fixed when it is declared. The type decides how many bytes it occupies, what values it can hold and how arithmetic on it behaves.

Declaring and initialising
    int count = 0;        /* declaration with initialisation */
    double gain;          /* declared, value indeterminate */
    gain = 2.5;           /* assignment */
A local variable that is not initialised holds an unpredictable value, so always initialise before reading.

The basic types
- char: one byte by definition; holds a character code ('A' is 65 in ASCII) and is really a small integer.
- short, int, long, long long: integers. The standard only fixes minimum sizes: int is at least 16 bits (32 bits on a typical PC, but 16 bits on 8-bit AVR microcontrollers), long at least 32, long long at least 64.
- float and double: floating-point numbers, typically 32-bit (about 7 significant decimal digits) and 64-bit (about 15 to 16 digits). Use double unless memory or speed forces float.
- unsigned versions hold only non-negative values: an 8-bit unsigned value ranges over 0 to 255, a signed one over -128 to 127.
- <stdint.h> gives exact-width types such as uint8_t, int16_t and uint32_t. These matter in embedded code, where you must match register sizes exactly.
- sizeof(type) gives the size in bytes; on a typical 64-bit PC sizeof(char) is 1, sizeof(int) is 4 and sizeof(double) is 8.

Arithmetic rules that catch people out
- Integer division truncates towards zero: 7 / 2 is 3 and -7 / 2 is -3. The remainder operator gives -7 % 2 equal to -1.
- The type of an expression is decided by its operands, not by where the result is stored. double r = 7 / 2; stores 3.0, because 7 / 2 is done in int arithmetic first.
- If either operand is floating point, the other is converted: 7 / 2.0 is 3.5. A cast forces this: (double)a / b.
- Converting a double to an int discards the fractional part: int n = 3.99; gives 3.
- Unsigned arithmetic wraps round modulo 2 to the power n: a uint8_t holding 250 becomes 4 after adding 10. Signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so never rely on it.
- Floating-point values are approximations: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false for doubles, so compare with a tolerance, e.g. fabs(a - b) < 1e-9.

A tested example (output on a 64-bit PC)
    int a = 7, b = 2;
    double r1 = a / b;            /* 3.000000 */
    double r2 = (double)a / b;    /* 3.500000 */
    uint8_t x = 250;  x += 10;    /* 4 */
    char c = 'A' + 2;             /* 'C' */

Constants
- const double VREF = 3.3; makes a read-only variable.
- #define N 10 is a preprocessor text substitution with no type.
- 'a' is a single char; "a" is a string of two bytes, 'a' followed by the terminating '\0'.

Exam tips: in any "what is printed" question, work out the type of every sub-expression before you calculate, and watch for integer division and unsigned wrap-around.

notes.h: Pointers, addresses and passing by reference
notes.body:
A pointer is a variable that holds the memory address of another object. Pointers let functions change their callers' variables, let you walk through arrays efficiently, and are how you reach dynamic memory and hardware registers.

The two operators
    int x = 10;
    int *p = &x;    /* p holds the address of x */
    *p = 20;        /* write through p: x is now 20 */
- &x gives the address of x.
- In a declaration, int *p says p is a pointer to int. In an expression, *p dereferences p, meaning "the int that p points to".
- printf("%p", (void *)p) prints an address.
- NULL is a pointer that points to nothing. Dereferencing it is undefined behaviour (usually a crash), so check before use.

C passes everything by value
A function gets copies of its arguments, so this swap does nothing to the caller:
    void swap_wrong(int a, int b) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; }
Pass the addresses instead, and work through them:
    void swap(int *a, int *b) { int t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t; }
    swap(&x, &y);
This is what "pass by reference" means in C: the address is still copied, but through it the function reaches the original variable. In a tested run, x = 1, y = 2 stays 1 2 after swap_wrong and becomes 2 1 after swap.

Because the pointer itself is a copy, changing the pointer inside the function (p = NULL;) does not affect the caller, whereas changing what it points to (*p = ...) does.

Pointers and arrays
- An array name used in an expression becomes a pointer to its first element: with int a[] = {10, 20, 30, 40}, a is &a[0].
- Pointer arithmetic counts in elements, not bytes: p + 1 points to the next int, whatever sizeof(int) is.
- a[i] is defined as *(a + i).
- Example: int *p = a + 1; points to 20. Then *(p + 2) is 40, while *p + 2 is 22, because * binds more tightly than +.

Pointers to structs
- p->field is shorthand for (*p).field. Passing a pointer to a large struct avoids copying it; add const if the function only reads it.

const and pointers
- const int *p: you cannot change the int through p, but p itself can be moved.
- int *const p: p cannot be moved, but the int can be changed.

Common bugs
- Uninitialised ("wild") pointers: int *p; *p = 5; writes to a random address.
- Dereferencing NULL.
- Returning the address of a local variable: it no longer exists after the function returns (a dangling pointer).
- Forgetting & in scanf, so scanf writes to an address made from a garbage value.

Exam tips: draw boxes for variables and arrows for pointers when tracing code; for every * ask whether it is part of a declaration or a dereference.

notes.body:
A microcontroller is a small computer on one chip: a processor core, flash memory for the program, a little RAM and built-in peripherals such as digital input/output (GPIO) pins, timers, analogue-to-digital converters and serial ports. C is the dominant language for programming them because it gives direct control of memory and hardware with little overhead.

From source to running hardware
- Cross-compilation: you compile on a PC for a different processor, using a toolchain for that target (for example arm-none-eabi-gcc for ARM Cortex-M parts, or avr-gcc for AVR chips).
- Linking uses start-up code and a linker script that describe where flash and RAM sit in the chip's memory map.
- The output (a binary or hex file) is flashed (programmed) into the chip's memory through a USB bootloader or a debug probe, and the chip runs it from reset.
- Environments such as the Arduino IDE hide these steps: you write setup() and loop(), and the framework supplies main.

How embedded programs differ
- There is usually no operating system, so main never returns. The usual structure is a "super-loop":
    int main(void)
    {
        init_hardware();
        while (1) {
            read_inputs();
            update_outputs();
        }
    }
- printf may not be available; debugging uses an LED, a serial (UART) link to the PC or a hardware debugger with breakpoints.
- RAM is measured in kilobytes, so use small fixed-width types (uint8_t, uint16_t), fixed-size arrays and few recursive calls, and avoid malloc.
- int may be only 16 bits on small 8-bit chips, which changes overflow behaviour; <stdint.h> types remove the doubt.
- Floating point may be slow if the chip has no hardware floating-point unit, because the compiler then emulates it in software.

Talking to hardware: registers
Peripherals are controlled through registers that appear at fixed memory addresses (memory-mapped I/O). Vendor header files define names for them; underneath, a register is accessed through a volatile pointer to a fixed address.
- volatile tells the compiler that the value can change outside the normal program flow (hardware, or an interrupt routine) and that every read and write must really happen. Without it the optimiser might keep a copy in a CPU register, or delete a write it thinks is unused.
- volatile does not make an access atomic; sharing multi-byte data with an interrupt may still need interrupts disabled briefly.

Bit manipulation
Each bit of a register usually controls one pin or setting, so you change single bits without disturbing the others:
- Set bit n: reg |= (1u << n);
- Clear bit n: reg &= ~(1u << n);
- Toggle bit n: reg ^= (1u << n);
- Test bit n: if (reg & (1u << n)) ...
Tested on a uint8_t starting at 0x00: setting bit 3 gives 0x08, setting bit 0 gives 0x09, toggling bit 3 gives 0x01 and clearing bit 0 gives 0x00. Bits are numbered from 0 at the least significant end.

Timing and events
- A busy-wait delay loop wastes processor time and depends on the clock speed; hardware timers are more accurate.
- Interrupts let hardware call an interrupt service routine (ISR) when something happens, such as a pin changing or a timer expiring. Keep ISRs short, and declare variables shared with main volatile.
- Mechanical buttons "bounce", producing several transitions in a few milliseconds, so inputs are debounced in software (for example by requiring a stable reading over several samples).

Exam tips: practise set, clear, toggle and test expressions on hexadecimal values by writing out the binary, and be ready to explain what volatile does and does not guarantee.

cards.b: The preprocessor copies the header's contents into the source file, giving the declarations (prototypes) of standard I/O functions such as printf and scanf. It does not contain their compiled code.
An int passed back to the operating system: 0 means success, non-zero indicates an error.
Preprocesses, compiles and assembles prog.c into an object file prog.o without linking.
A link-time error: the code compiled but the linker could not find sqrt's definition. With gcc on many Linux systems you must link the maths library with -lm.
Compiler options that turn on extra warnings about suspicious code (unused variables, implicit fall-through, type mismatches in printf, etc.).

cards.f: Format specifier for a size_t (e.g. sizeof result)
cards.b: %zu
scanf must store the value in x, so it needs x's address; passing x itself would pass a copy of its (garbage) value.
Compile-time: the compiler rejects the code (syntax/type errors), so no executable. Run-time: the program builds but crashes or produces wrong results when run.
7 / 2 is 3 (integer division truncates); 7 / 2.0 is 3.5 because the int is converted to double.
3.0. The division is done in int arithmetic before the result is converted to double.

cards.f: Minimum size of int guaranteed by the C standard
cards.b: 16 bits. It is usually 32 bits on PCs but 16 bits on 8-bit AVR microcontrollers, so use <stdint.h> types when size matters.

cards.f: uint8_t x = 250; x += 10; value of x?
cards.b: 4: unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 256 (260 - 256).
Undefined behaviour in C: the program may do anything, so it must be avoided (unlike unsigned wrap-around, which is well defined).
-3 and -1: division truncates towards zero and the remainder takes the sign of the dividend.
'a' is one char (an integer code). "a" is a string literal: an array of 2 chars, 'a' and the terminator '\0'.
Floating-point values are binary approximations (0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3), so compare |a - b| against a small tolerance.
0 to N - 1. C does no bounds checking; accessing v[N] is undefined behaviour.
0. Elements without an initialiser are set to zero when any initialiser list is given.
C stores a 2-D array row by row: m[i][j] in an array with C columns lies i × C + j elements from m[0][0].

cards.f: Passing a 2-D array to a function
cards.b: All dimensions except the first must be stated, e.g. void f(int m[][4], int rows); so the compiler can compute row offsets.

cards.f: sizeof and strlen of char s[] = "EEE"
cards.b: sizeof s is 4 (includes the '\0' terminator); strlen(s) is 3.
(*p).x: access member x of the struct that pointer p points to.

cards.f: Why sizeof(struct) may exceed the sum of its members
cards.b: The compiler adds padding so members are aligned in memory; e.g. {char c; int i;} is typically 8 bytes, not 5.

cards.f: Why sizeof v / sizeof v[0] fails inside a function
cards.b: An array parameter is really a pointer, so sizeof gives the pointer's size. Pass the length as a separate argument.
while tests before the body (may run 0 times); do-while tests after it, so the body always runs at least once.
Without break, execution continues into the next case's statements until a break or the end of the switch.

cards.f: Number of passes: for (i = 0; i <= n; i++)
cards.b: n + 1 (i takes the values 0, 1, ..., n).
= assigns 5 to x, so the condition is 5 (true) every time. Equality is tested with ==.
&& stops if the left operand is false; || stops if it is true. So (p != NULL && p->v > 0) never dereferences a NULL p.
break exits the innermost loop or switch; continue jumps straight to the next iteration (to the update in a for loop).

cards.f: Allowed type of a switch expression
cards.b: An integer type (including char and enum); case labels must be integer constant expressions.
A declaration giving return type, name and parameter types, ending in ';'. It lets the compiler check calls made before the definition appears.
The function receives copies of the arguments; changing a parameter does not change the caller's variable.
Initialised once and keeps its value between calls, but is visible only inside its function.

cards.f: Why functions can modify array arguments
cards.b: Passing an array passes the address of its first element, so the function works on the caller's elements, not a copy.
The condition in which a recursive function returns without calling itself, guaranteeing the recursion ends.

cards.f: Two ways to return several results from a C function
cards.b: Pass pointers to variables the function fills in (output parameters), or return a struct holding all the results.
Holds declarations (prototypes, struct definitions, #defines) shared between .c files via #include; definitions go in .c files.
The address of x (address-of operator).
Dereference: the object p points to. It can be read or assigned (*p = 5).

cards.f: Does C have pass by reference?
cards.b: No: all arguments are passed by value. Passing a pointer copies the address, which lets the function change the object it points to.
*(a + i): pointer arithmetic moves i elements (not bytes) from the start.
*(p + 2) is 40 (element a[3]); *p + 2 is 22 (20 + 2), because * binds more tightly than +.
A pointer to memory that no longer exists, e.g. the address of a local variable after its function returns, or memory already freed.
const int *p: the pointed-to int cannot be changed through p. int *const p: the pointer itself cannot be changed.
A pointer value meaning 'points to nothing'. Initialise pointers to NULL and check before dereferencing.
NULL. Always check before using the pointer.
malloc(bytes) leaves contents indeterminate; calloc(count, size) allocates count × size bytes and zeroes them.

cards.f: Allocate an array of n doubles
cards.b: double *v = malloc(n * sizeof *v);  (equivalently n * sizeof(double)), then check v != NULL.

cards.f: Why not write p = realloc(p, size);
cards.b: If realloc fails it returns NULL and the old block is still allocated; overwriting p loses the only pointer to it, causing a leak.
Allocated memory that can no longer be freed because every pointer to it has been lost or overwritten.
Accessing a block after it has been freed: undefined behaviour. Setting the pointer to NULL after free helps catch it.
Stack: automatic local variables, freed automatically on return. Heap: malloc'd blocks that persist until free is called.
Small RAM and heap fragmentation can make allocation fail unpredictably; standards such as MISRA C forbid it, so fixed-size buffers are used.
A struct containing a pointer to its own type, e.g. struct node { int data; struct node *next; }; used to build lists and trees.
It must change the caller's head pointer; a struct node * parameter would be a copy, so the caller's head would not change.

cards.f: Safe way to free a linked list
cards.b: Loop: save next = p->next, free(p), then p = next. Reading p->next after free(p) is undefined behaviour.
All keys in a node's left subtree are smaller than its key; all keys in its right subtree are larger.
Left subtree, node, right subtree; visits keys in ascending order.

cards.f: Which traversal frees a tree safely?
cards.b: Post-order (left, right, node): children are freed before their parent, so no freed node is read.
n (a chain), e.g. when keys are inserted in sorted order; search then takes O(n), like a list.

cards.f: Deleting a BST node with two children
cards.b: Replace its key with the in-order successor (minimum of the right subtree) and delete that successor node instead.
A compiler that runs on one machine (e.g. a PC) but produces code for a different processor, such as an ARM Cortex-M microcontroller.
The usual bare-metal structure: initialise hardware, then repeat forever in while (1); main never returns because there is no OS.

cards.f: Set, clear and toggle bit n of reg
cards.b: Set: reg |= (1u << n); clear: reg &= ~(1u << n); toggle: reg ^= (1u << n).

cards.f: Test whether bit n of reg is 1
cards.b: if (reg & (1u << n)) — the result is non-zero exactly when bit n is set.
Forces the compiler to perform every read and write of the variable as written, because it may change outside normal program flow (hardware or ISR).
It does not make accesses atomic or prevent race conditions; shared multi-byte data may still need interrupts briefly disabled.
Peripheral registers appear at fixed memory addresses, so C reads and writes them through (volatile) pointers like ordinary variables.
A mechanical contact makes several rapid transitions when pressed; software debouncing waits for a stable reading before acting.

questions.q: A program uses sqrt(x) on a value read with scanf and #includes <math.h>. On a Linux machine, gcc prog.c -o prog prints "undefined reference to `sqrt'". At which stage did the build fail?
questions.why: The message comes from the linker: the call compiled because math.h declared sqrt, but the linker was not told to search the maths library, so the fix is to add -lm. A preprocessing failure would be a complaint that a header file could not be found, not a missing definition. A compilation failure would be a syntax or type error in the source, but here the source was valid. Run time is impossible because no executable was produced.

questions.q: Which gcc command produces an object file (.o) from prog.c without linking?
questions.why: -c runs the preprocessor, compiler and assembler and stops before linking, leaving prog.o. -E stops after preprocessing and prints the expanded source. -S stops after compilation and writes assembly (prog.s), one stage too early. Building with -o prog goes all the way through linking to an executable.

questions.q: Describe the four stages gcc goes through to turn hello.c into an executable, and give one example of an error that would be reported at the compilation stage and one at the linking stage.
markScheme: Preprocessing: handles # directives, e.g. #include copies header text in, #define macros expanded
Compilation: syntax and type checking, translation to assembly
Assembly: assembly converted to machine code in an object file (.o)
Linking: object files combined with library code to give an executable
Correct examples: compile error such as a missing semicolon or undeclared variable; link error such as undefined reference to a misspelt function or a missing library (e.g. -lm)
questions.modelAnswer: First the preprocessor deals with lines beginning with #: #include <stdio.h> copies in the header's declarations and #define macros are replaced. The compiler then checks the syntax and types and translates the C into assembly for the target processor. The assembler converts that into machine code in an object file, hello.o. Finally the linker joins the object file with library code, such as the compiled printf, and resolves every function call to produce the executable. A missing semicolon or using an undeclared variable is reported by the compiler. Calling a function that is declared but never defined, such as a misspelt prnt or sqrt without -lm on Linux, compiles but fails at linking with "undefined reference".

questions.why: 7 / 2 has two int operands, so it is integer division giving 3, which is then converted to 3.0 and printed to one decimal place. 3.5 assumes the division happens in double because the result is stored in a double, but the operand types decide that. 4.0 assumes the result is rounded, but integer division truncates. 3 forgets that %.1f always prints one decimal place.

options: Nothing reliable: this is undefined behaviour
questions.why: uint8_t holds 0 to 255 and unsigned values wrap modulo 256, so 260 becomes 4. 260 ignores the 8-bit width of the variable. 255 assumes the value saturates at the maximum, which C does not do. Undefined behaviour applies to signed overflow; unsigned wrap-around is fully defined by the standard.

markScheme: x = 3.0: int / int is integer division (3) before conversion to double
y = 3.5: the cast makes a a double, so b is converted and real division is used
z = -1: remainder has the sign of the dividend because division truncates towards zero
n = 9: converting double to int discards the fractional part (no rounding)
questions.modelAnswer: x is 3.0 because a / b is evaluated with two ints, giving 3, and only then converted to double. y is 3.5 because (double)a is a double, so b is promoted and floating-point division gives 3.5. z is -1: -7 / 2 truncates to -3, and -7 - (-3 × 2) = -1. n is 9 because assigning a double to an int simply drops the fractional part; it does not round to 10.

questions.q: Given int m[3][4];, how many int elements from m[0][0] is m[2][1] stored?
questions.why: C uses row-major order, so the offset is row × (number of columns) + column = 2 × 4 + 1 = 9. 7 multiplies by the number of rows (3) instead of the row length (4). 5 is the column-major offset, 1 × 3 + 2, which is how Fortran or MATLAB would store it, not C. 10 is the element's position counting from 1 (it is the tenth element), not its offset from the start.

questions.q: On a 64-bit PC, what does sizeof(s) give for char s[] = "UCL";?
questions.why: The array holds 'U', 'C', 'L' and the terminating '\0', so it is 4 bytes. 3 is what strlen returns because it does not count the terminator. 8 is the size of a pointer on a 64-bit machine, which would be the answer for char *s, not for an array. 1 is the size of a single char.

questions.q: Define a struct type for a sensor sample holding an integer channel number and a double voltage. Then write a function that takes an array of n samples and returns the mean voltage.
markScheme: Correct struct definition with int and double members (optionally with typedef)
Function signature taking the array (or pointer) and the count n separately
Accumulator of type double initialised to 0
Loop over indices 0 to n - 1 using the dot operator to read each voltage
Returns total / n (and ideally guards against n < 1 or documents it)

questions.why: Execution jumps to case 2, prints b, falls through into case 3 because there is no break, prints c and then stops at the break. Answering just b forgets fall-through. bcd ignores the break after case 3, which ends the switch before default. abc assumes the switch runs from the top, but it jumps directly to the matching label.

questions.q: How many times does the body of for (i = 0; i <= 10; i += 2) run?
questions.why: i takes the values 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, which is 6 passes; the test then fails at 12. 5 comes from dividing 10 by the step of 2, which counts the gaps between values rather than the values themselves. 11 ignores the step and counts as if i went up by 1. 7 counts the final test at i = 12 as a pass, but the body does not run when the test fails.

questions.q: Write a C fragment that repeatedly asks the user for an integer until they enter a value from 1 to 5, and explain why a do-while loop is the natural choice.
markScheme: Uses do { ... } while (...) with the prompt and scanf inside the body
Correct condition: repeat while value < 1 || value > 5
Uses &value in scanf (and ideally checks scanf's return value)
Explanation: the body must run at least once before there is anything to test

options: Nothing: it does not compile, because a static variable cannot be modified
questions.why: c is static, so it is initialised once and keeps its value: the three calls return 1, 2 and 3, and the third is printed. 1 would be right if c were an ordinary local variable reset to 0 on every call. 2 counts only the two calls made before the printf, but the call inside printf also increments c. Saying it does not compile confuses static with const: static changes how long c lives, not whether it can be modified.

f(4) = 4 × f(3) = 4 × 3 × f(2) = 4 × 3 × 2 × f(1) = 24. 10 adds the numbers (4 + 3 + 2 + 1) instead of multiplying them. 12 stops one level early, as if the base case returned 1 at n = 2, and so loses the factor 2. 6 is f(3), an off-by-one in counting the levels of recursion.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a function declaration and a function definition in C. Why does a program that calls average() in main, but defines average() after main, need a declaration above main?
markScheme: Definition contains the body and creates the function's code
Declaration (prototype) gives only return type, name and parameter types, ending with a semicolon
The compiler reads the file top to bottom and must know the signature at the point of the call
So it can check argument number and types and the return type; modern C (C99 onwards) does not allow calls to undeclared functions
questions.modelAnswer: A definition gives the complete function, including its body, and is where its code comes from. A declaration, or prototype, such as double average(const double v[], int n); states only the return type, the name and the parameter types. The compiler processes the file from top to bottom, so when it reaches the call in main it must already know average's signature in order to check the arguments and know what type comes back. Since C99, calling a function with no declaration in scope is not allowed, so the prototype is placed above main or in an included header.

options: Nothing: the program crashes when printing x
questions.why: f doubles the int that p points to, so x becomes 10. Setting p = NULL only changes f's own copy of the address, so x is unaffected. 5 assumes the function cannot change x, but it was given x's address. 0 assumes p = NULL sets x to zero, confusing the pointer with the value it points to. There is no crash, because after p = NULL nothing dereferences p, and main prints the int x, not a pointer.

options: Nothing: you cannot add an integer to a pointer
questions.why: p points to a[1] (20). *(p + 2) moves two elements on to a[3], which is 40. *p + 2 dereferences first, because * binds more tightly than +, giving 20 + 2 = 22. 22 40 swaps the two precedence rules. 30 12 treats p as pointing to a[0], ignoring the + 1. Adding an integer to a pointer is legal pointer arithmetic and moves by whole elements.

questions.q: Write a function swap that exchanges the values of two int variables in the caller, show how it is called, and explain why a version declared void swap(int a, int b) cannot work.
markScheme: Signature takes two int pointers: void swap(int *a, int *b)
Body uses a temporary and dereferences: t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t;
Call passes addresses: swap(&x, &y);
Explanation: C passes arguments by value, so the int version only swaps local copies
Notes that passing pointers lets the function reach the original variables

questions.q: Which line correctly allocates space for n values of type double?
questions.why: malloc takes a size in bytes, so n doubles need n × sizeof(double) bytes, and the result must be stored in a pointer. malloc(n) requests only n bytes, an eighth of what is needed when a double is 8 bytes. malloc(sizeof(double)) gives room for a single double. Storing the result in double v instead of a pointer is a type error: malloc returns an address.

options: It returns the address of a local array that no longer exists after the function returns
It leaks memory because buf is never freed
It will not compile because C functions cannot return arrays
Nothing: arrays are passed by reference so the caller gets a valid copy
questions.why: buf is an automatic variable, so its storage is reclaimed when the function returns and the caller is left with a dangling pointer; the fix is to malloc the buffer and have the caller free it. There is no leak, because automatic variables are released automatically and free is only for heap memory. It does compile, because the array decays to an int * and the function returns that pointer (gcc gives a warning). No copy is made: only the address is returned, which is exactly the problem.

questions.q: Explain, with a short code example of each, what a memory leak and a dangling pointer are, and state one practice that prevents each.
markScheme: Leak defined: allocated block whose last pointer is lost without free
Valid leak example, e.g. p = malloc(...); p = malloc(...); or returning without free
Dangling pointer defined: pointer to memory that has been freed or has gone out of scope
Valid dangling example, e.g. free(p); *p = 3; or returning address of a local
Prevention: free every allocation on every exit path / use valgrind; set pointer to NULL after free / don't return addresses of locals
questions.modelAnswer:
A memory leak happens when a block is allocated but every pointer to it is lost before free is called, for example:
int *p = malloc(100 * sizeof *p);
p = malloc(200 * sizeof *p);   /* first block now unreachable */
The first block can never be freed. Prevent it by pairing every malloc with a free on every path out of the function and by checking with valgrind.
A dangling pointer points to memory that is no longer valid, for example:
free(p);
p[0] = 3;   /* use after free */
Prevent it by setting p = NULL immediately after free(p), and never returning the address of a local variable.

questions.q: Starting from an empty list, push_front is called with 5, then 8, then 1. What does printing the list from the head give?
questions.why: Each new node goes in front of the old head, so the last value pushed is first: 1 8 5. 5 8 1 is the order of insertion, which you would get by appending at the tail. 1 5 8 assumes the list keeps itself sorted, but push_front does no ordering. A list holding only 1 is what a buggy version would give if it set head to the new node without first linking n->next to the old head.

questions.q: Keys are inserted into an empty BST in the order 40, 20, 60, 10, 30, 50, 70. What is the pre-order traversal?
questions.why: Pre-order visits the node, then its left subtree, then its right: 40, then the subtree rooted at 20 (20, 10, 30), then the subtree rooted at 60 (60, 50, 70). The sorted sequence is the in-order traversal. 10 30 20 50 70 60 40 is post-order, with each node after its children. 40 20 60 10 30 50 70 is level order (breadth-first), which here also equals the insertion order.

Count works for the empty list (returns 0)

questions.why: 0x5A is 0101 1010. Setting bit 0 gives 0101 1011 (0x5B), and clearing bit 4 gives 0100 1011, which is 0x4B. 0x10 comes from leaving out the ~, so the mask keeps only bit 4 instead of clearing it. 0x4A misses the effect of the first line, as if OR-ing in bit 0 changed nothing. 0x53 clears bit 3 instead of bit 4, which happens if you read 1u << 4 as the fourth bit counting from 1 (0x08) rather than bit 4 counting from 0 (0x10).

questions.q: Why should a flag that an interrupt service routine sets and the main loop polls be declared volatile?
options: So reads and writes to it are atomic and cannot be interrupted
So it is stored in non-volatile flash and survives a power cut
So it becomes read-only and the ISR cannot corrupt it
So the compiler re-reads it from memory on every access instead of using a cached copy
questions.why: Without volatile the optimiser may load the flag into a register once and loop on that copy, never seeing the ISR's change; volatile forces a real memory access each time. Atomic access is not what volatile provides: a multi-byte variable can still be torn by an interrupt. Non-volatile flash is unrelated, because the keyword is about compiler optimisation, not the type of memory. Making something read-only is what const does, and the ISR needs to write the flag anyway.

questions.q: Describe the steps needed to get a C program written on a PC running on a microcontroller, and give three ways in which writing C for a microcontroller differs from writing it for a PC.
markScheme: Cross-compile with a toolchain for the target processor
Link with start-up code/linker script matching the chip's memory map, producing a binary/hex image
Flash the image to the chip (bootloader or debug probe) and run/debug it
Differences (any three): no OS so main never returns / super-loop; very limited RAM so fixed-size data and no malloc; direct register access with volatile and bit manipulation
Further valid differences: int size may be 16 bits so use stdint types; limited or no printf so debug via LED/UART/debugger; floating point may be slow without an FPU; interrupts
questions.modelAnswer:
The code is compiled on the PC with a cross-compiler for the target processor, such as arm-none-eabi-gcc for an ARM Cortex-M. It is linked with start-up code and a linker script describing where the chip's flash and RAM are, producing a binary or hex image. That image is flashed into the microcontroller through a USB bootloader or a debug probe, and the chip runs it from reset; a debugger or a serial link can then be used to test it.
Differences: (1) there is usually no operating system, so main never returns and the program is a while (1) super-loop; (2) RAM is tiny, so you use fixed-size arrays and small fixed-width types and normally avoid malloc; (3) hardware is controlled by reading and writing memory-mapped registers through volatile pointers, using bit masks to change single bits.

(b) Write a function int stats(const Sample *s, int n, double *mean, double *max) that returns 0 if n < 1 and otherwise returns 1 and passes back the mean and maximum voltage through the two pointer parameters. [7]

questions.q:
(a) Define a C struct for a binary search tree (BST) node holding an int key. [2]
(b) Write a recursive function that inserts a key into a BST and returns the (possibly new) root, ignoring duplicates. [6]
(c) Keys are inserted into an empty tree in the order 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 35. Draw the tree and give its in-order, pre-order and post-order traversals and its height (counting nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path). [6]
(d) How many key comparisons does an iterative search make to find 35, and to discover that 65 is absent? [2]
(e) Write a function to free the whole tree and explain why its traversal order matters. Comment on what happens to search time if the keys are inserted in ascending order. [4]
markScheme: (a) struct with int key and left/right pointers to the same struct type
(b) Base case: NULL root → malloc a node, check NULL, set key and both children to NULL, return it
(b) Recursive case: go left if key < root->key, right if greater, assign the result back to the child pointer; return root
(c) Correct tree: 50 root; 30 (20, 40 with left child 35); 70 (60, 80)
(d) 35: 4 comparisons (50, 30, 40, 35); 65: 3 comparisons (50, 70, 60) then NULL
(e) Post-order free, because children must be released before the parent's pointers are lost
(e) Sorted insertion gives a chain of height n, so search degrades from about log2 n to n comparisons
